introScreens.headline: What Really Happened on Mars in 2018
introScreens.bodyText: In late May 2018, a NASA spacecraft orbiting Mars spotted a small swirling dust storm. Within three weeks, high-altitude winds whipped it into a monster storm wrapping around the entire planet—rising more than 37 miles high, seven times higher than an airplane flies on Earth. Dust blocked 97% of the sunlight so noon turned pitch black: NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover lost battery power and never woke up, while Curiosity kept working on a small nuclear battery.
introScreens.nasaSource: NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter & Mars Exploration Rover Mission Archives (2018)

introScreens.headline: NASA's Next Big Step: Moon to Mars
introScreens.bodyText: Through the Moon to Mars program, NASA is preparing the first human missions to live and work on the Red Planet. Real astronauts will need nonstop electricity every Martian Sol to run oxygen generators, keep habitat rooms warm in -90°F nights, and keep liquid rocket fuel cold for their ride home. Because global storms erupt every few Mars years, NASA is developing compact nuclear fission power so bases never rely on sunlight alone.
introScreens.nasaSource: NASA Moon to Mars Architecture & Fission Surface Power Studies

introScreens.headline: Future Mission (May 2038): What Would You Do?
introScreens.bodyText: Now fast-forward to May 2038 at Ares Base, a four-astronaut outpost powered by giant solar wings and a compact Kilopower backup unit. Based on what happened in 2018, if astronauts face a similar Planet-Encircling Dust Event in the future, what would you do? Across a 100x thinner Martian air and a 22-minute radio delay, shutting gear down only conserves remaining energy—only sunlight or nuclear fission can generate new power!
introScreens.nasaSource: Future 2038 Scenario Built From Real Mars Year 34 (2018) Storm Data

kidGlossary.headline: May 30, 2018: Spotted From Mars Orbit
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On May 30, 2018, NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed a small dust cloud near Perseverance Valley. Within days it exploded into a planet-wide blackout—showing future 2038 crews why orbital weather cams give crucial early warning.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A dust storm on Mars starts when sunlight heats thin air near the ground, lifting rusty red powder into spinning clouds that can grow and merge.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter captured this daily global map showing a fast-growing Martian dust storm cloud spreading across Perseverance Valley.

kidGlossary.headline: 2018 Storm Towered 37 Miles High
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA's Mars Climate Sounder tracked high-altitude winds lifting red dust over 37 miles (60 km) into the sky—seven times higher than passenger jets fly on Earth—hiding even Mars's giant volcanoes from space cameras.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: 37 miles (60 kilometers) is about seven times higher than passenger airplanes fly on Earth—meaning dust soared way above normal clouds into high skies.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: An orbital view over Mars reveals how towering dust plumes rose more than 37 miles into the sky and blurred giant volcanoes beneath.

kidGlossary.headline: Why Solar-Powered Opportunity Shut Down
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Opportunity explored Mars for over 14 years using solar wings. During the June 2018 storm, dust blocked 97% of sunlight, its batteries drained in freezing darkness, and NASA ended the mission after 1,000+ recovery pings went unanswered.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Opportunity was a golf-cart-sized NASA robot rover powered by two flat solar wings that soaked up sunlight to charge its batteries on Mars.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A NASA photograph of the Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity with its twin solar array wings spread wide to gather Martian sunlight.

kidGlossary.headline: Curiosity's Nuclear Battery (MMRTG)
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Across Mars in Gale Crater, Curiosity never missed a day of science during the 2018 blackout because technicians installed an MMRTG—a sealed nuclear battery that turns steady heat into electricity without needing sunlight.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Unlike solar rovers, NASA's Curiosity rover did not shut down during the 2018 blackness because it makes electricity from heat inside a sealed nuclear battery.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA technicians at Kennedy Space Center install Curiosity's Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG) nuclear power unit before launch.

kidGlossary.headline: A Martian Sol: 24 Hours, 39 Minutes
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: One day on Mars is called a Sol and lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes—almost an Earth day, yet just different enough that NASA flight crews and future Mars astronauts live on shifting 'Mars Time' schedules.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A Sol is one full day-and-night rotation on Mars: 24 hours and 39 minutes—just 39 minutes longer than a day on Earth.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's InSight lander instruments sit on rusty Martian soil where every sunrise and sunset marks another 24-hour-39-minute Martian Sol.

kidGlossary.headline: Mars Physics: 100x Thinner Martian Air
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Mars's atmosphere is 100 times thinner than Earth's! Even a 60 mph Martian dust storm pushes like a gentle breeze—so wind won't blow down future habitats, though microscopic dust still blankets panels and seals.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Mars has very little air around it—only about 1% as thick as Earth's atmosphere—so even fast 60 mph winds push softly like a light breeze.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A thin blue-tinted slice of Mars's wispy atmosphere photographed from orbit—too thin to knock down habitats, yet able to carry powdery dust.

kidGlossary.headline: 2018 Challenge: Static-Cling Dust
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Martian dust grains are finer than baby powder and carry static electric charge—clinging to Opportunity's solar panels like dust on a rubbed balloon and sneaking into rover wheel joints.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Martian soil is crushed into powder finer than baby powder that holds static electricity, making grains cling tightly to visor glass, gaskets, and solar wings.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Close-up microscopic view of fine red Martian grit photographed by NASA's Opportunity rover while exploring Meridiani Planum.

kidGlossary.headline: June 10, 2018: Pitch Black at Noon
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 10, 2018, suspended dust above Opportunity reached a record opacity (tau > 10.8), blocking 97% of sunlight so high noon looked darker than a moonless night on Earth.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Even at 12:00 PM midday when the Sun is directly overhead, airborne dust can get so thick that 97% of light is blocked and noon looks darker than midnight.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A NASA sunlight simulation showing how clear noon on Mars on the left plunged into pitch darkness on June 10, 2018 on the right.

kidGlossary.headline: Keeping Return Rocket Fuel Cryogenic
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Future Mars Ascent Vehicles need nonstop electric chillers to keep liquid oxygen and methane propellant super-cold (-297°F). Without power during a storm, rocket fuel slowly warms and boils off.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Return rockets use cryogenic liquid fuel chilled below -297°F (-183°C); if electrical coolers stop running, that icy liquid warms up and boils away as gas.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA orbital cooling hardware designed to test how super-cold liquid rocket propellant can be stored without warming and boiling away.

kidGlossary.headline: The 2018 Heat-Blanket Surprise
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA instruments proved a strange twist in 2018: while thick dust made Mars days cooler by blocking sunlight, nights actually got WARMER because suspended dust trapped surface heat like a giant red blanket!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Thick clouds of floating dust act like a bedroom blanket over Mars: blocking daytime sunlight while trapping nighttime ground warmth from escaping into space.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Curiosity rover photos from the June 2018 global storm showing dimmed afternoon light while thick dust trapped heat near the ground at night.

kidGlossary.headline: Deep Space Network Radio Delay
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Radio signals between Mars and NASA's giant Deep Space Network dishes on Earth take 6 to 22 minutes one way—up to 44 minutes just to ask Mission Control for advice and hear back!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Mars and Earth are millions of miles apart, so radio messages traveling at light speed take up to 22 minutes one way—you cannot phone Mission Control live.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: One of NASA's giant 70-meter Deep Space Network dish antennas that beams and receives radio signals between Earth and Mars.

kidGlossary.headline: June 20, 2018: Planet-Encircling Dust Event
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 20, 2018, NASA officially upgraded the storm to a Planet-Encircling Dust Event (PEDE)—one continuous orange dust shroud wrapping all 360 degrees around Mars at once.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A Planet-Encircling Dust Event means a storm has grown so huge that thick swirling orange dust wraps completely around every side of Mars at once.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Two NASA global views of Mars taken weeks apart in 2018: clear craters before the storm on the left, and a planet-wide dust blanket on the right.

kidGlossary.headline: Dust Devils & Lucky Cleaning Events
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: In earlier years, Spirit and Opportunity rovers sometimes survived dusty winters when tiny Martian whirlwinds—dust devils—swept panels clean, though no lucky gust rescued Opportunity in 2018.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: A dust devil is a tiny spinning whirlwind on Mars that sometimes brushes across a rover and sweeps sticky red grit right off dusty solar panels.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A sunlit NASA rover photo showing a whirling Martian dust devil sweeping across crater plains like a natural broom.

kidGlossary.headline: Curiosity's Dusty June 15, 2018 Selfie
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 15, 2018, Curiosity snapped a murky orange self-portrait inside Gale Crater showing thick haze blotting out distant crater rims while its nuclear-powered science lab kept sampling the storm.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: On June 15, 2018, Curiosity held out its camera arm to snap a selfie inside Gale Crater while murky brown storm haze swallowed the distant mountain rim.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's Curiosity rover photographed itself on June 15, 2018, surrounded by thick brown dust haze while its nuclear battery kept tools running.

kidGlossary.headline: NASA Fission Surface Power
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: To protect human explorers from 2018-style blackouts, NASA Glenn Research Center is testing compact Fission Surface Power reactors that generate steady electricity day and night—even in weeks of total darkness.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Nuclear fission splits atoms inside a safe sealed core to produce steady electricity and heat day and night—even during weeks of dusty total darkness.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Concept artwork from NASA Glenn Research Center showing a Fission Surface Power reactor delivering nonstop electricity without sunlight.

kidGlossary.headline: MOXIE: Making Breathable Oxygen on Mars
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Mars's air is 95% carbon dioxide. NASA's gold-plated MOXIE experiment on the Perseverance rover proved a toaster-sized machine can split Martian air into pure breathable oxygen—just like a mechanical tree!
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Oxygen generators pull carbon dioxide gas out of Mars's air and electrochemically split off pure oxygen atoms so astronauts have clean air to breathe.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA's gold-coated MOXIE experiment aboard Perseverance—a real machine tested on Mars to turn carbon dioxide air into breathable oxygen.

kidGlossary.headline: Dust Storms Lift Water Skyward
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA's Mars Climate Sounder discovered that global dust storms heat the thin air and lift hidden water vapor 50 miles upward, where sunlight breaks water apart—showing why crews must protect base water loops.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Water vapor is invisible water gas floating in the air; global dust storms warm Mars's upper skies and carry water miles up where sunlight splits it apart.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: A NASA atmospheric map showing how Martian dust storms lift warm water vapor high above the surface into sunlight-exposed skies.

kidGlossary.headline: Designing Mars Base Greenhouses
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: At NASA's Kennedy Space Center MarsPort engineering forums, designers planned pressurized Martian greenhouses using grow-LEDs so crews can raise fresh food and boost morale when storms shut off outdoor light.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: Hydroponic greenhouses grow vegetables indoors using mineral-rich water and pink-purple LED grow lights instead of outdoor soil or natural sunlight.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: NASA greenhouse researchers testing leafy food crops under specialized indoor grow lights built for future off-world habitats.

kidGlossary.headline: Electrodynamic Dust Shields for Suits
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: At Kennedy Space Center's SwampWorks lab, engineers tested high-voltage wire grids that zap static-charged dust off spacesuits and airlock glass—keeping razor-fine Martian grit out of astronaut lungs.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: An electrostatic dust shield sends harmless tiny electrical waves across thin wires woven into glass or spacesuit fabric to push static-cling dust right off.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Engineers at NASA Kennedy Space Center testing an Electrodynamic Dust Shield that pulses electric fields to shake sticky dust off surfaces.

kidGlossary.headline: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Data Relay
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter acts like a giant sky tower—snapping wide storm photos and beaming surface radio signals cleanly back to Earth's antennas even through swirling dust clouds.
kidGlossary.termMeaning: An orbital relay is a satellite circling high above Mars that spots storm fronts from space and bounces radio messages between astronauts and Earth.
kidGlossary.imageCaption: Artist illustration of NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter circling Mars to capture storm maps and relay radio data back to Earth.

storyNodes.title: Sol 1: Orbital Storm Alarm
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: On May 30, 2018, NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted a local storm days before it swallowed the planet.
storyNodes.storyText: Overhead satellites just spotted a small swirling dust storm speeding toward Ares Base! The butterscotch sky is still bright this Martian Sol, and your astronauts are outside drilling deep ice cores while dust clouds lift rising water vapor on the horizon.

choiceA.description: Cancel outdoor drilling immediately, bring everyone inside, and pack max solar electricity into the battery vault.
choiceA.outcomeText: You scrub the ice drill early and fill your backup battery banks to bursting. The power grid looks solid, though losing weeks of science leaves the crew frustrated.
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: Opportunity explored Mars for 14+ years before 2018's storm starved its solar arrays. NASA beamed over 1,000 recovery commands over 8 months before concluding its mission in February 2019—inspiring hybrid nuclear-solar designs for 2038.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Once batteries drop too low in -90°F Martian darkness, unheated flight clocks and computers can reset permanently—just like Opportunity's final blackout.
choiceA.imageCaption: This artist's illustration shows NASA's InSight lander on the surface of Mars, with its solar arrays deployed.

choiceB.description: Let astronauts finish collecting core samples while cranking compressors to fill spare oxygen tanks.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your team celebrates securing priceless ice samples and brimmed oxygen tanks, though heavy pump motors noticeably drain battery reserves.
choiceB.nasaComparisonTitle: Kilopower Fission Surface Power vs. Solar
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Solar-powered Opportunity froze to death in 2018, whereas Curiosity's nuclear MMRTG ran non-stop. For future humans, NASA Glenn built the Kilopower (KRUSTY) fission reactor so astronauts have sunlight-independent electricity.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: Nuclear fission splits Uranium-235 atoms inside a shielded core—making it one of the ONLY ways to physically generate electricity in pitch-black darkness!
choiceB.imageCaption: An electrical cable can be seen snaking its way along insulation material in this image of the interior of the Mars 2020 spacecraft at it cruises through interplanetary space to the Red Planet.

choiceC.description: Bring astronauts indoors safely and spend battery charge deploying NASA KSC Electrodynamic Dust Shields across solar glass and airlocks.
choiceC.outcomeText: Transparent EDS electrodes pulse across your airlock visors and solar glass, shaking off static dust while draining modest grid charge.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: NASA KSC Electrodynamic Dust Shield & Suitports
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: At NASA's Kennedy Space Center SwampWorks lab, engineers invented the Electrodynamic Dust Shield (EDS)—transparent electrodes that push static-charged Martian dust away using high-voltage waves, paired with Suitport dust-lock doors.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Martian dust grains carry static electric charge like rubbed wool—making them cling to solar glass and threaten astronaut lungs if brought indoors.
choiceC.imageCaption: Partially obscured by the Canadarm2, or Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS), arm the Space Shuttle Atlantis (background) moves toward the International Space Station (ISS) during rendezvous operations.

storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: By June 3, 2018, rising dust forced NASA's Opportunity team to halt science driving and guard power.

consequences.text: Your Sol 1 battery overcharge keeps emergency power vaults topped off (+3% Electricity), though losing the early ice drill frustrated the crew (-3% Crew Health).

storyNodes.storyText: The storm wall reaches Ares Base, towering more than 37 miles high! Already sticky red grit clings to solar wings like static-charged powder, forcing you to balance cabin air against rocket tanks that must keep liquid rocket fuel cold.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Lock Fuel Chillers & Dim Hallway Heat
choiceA.description: Protect return rocket fuel coolers on max priority while dropping corridor thermostats to save extra grid watts.
choiceA.outcomeText: Fuel tanks stay icy cold and existing battery charge is conserved, though shivering hallways wear on your astronauts. Shutting down extra hardware conserves 100% of remaining battery charge for critical survival!
choiceA.nasaRealDecision: NASA's Mars Ascent Vehicle (MAV) studies show liquid methane and oxygen propellants require active cryocoolers. During a 2018-scale blackout, flight controllers must balance cooling propellant for launch against indoor life support.
choiceA.nasaFactEmphasis: Without cold temperatures (-297°F), liquid oxygen slowly warms and boils away—meaning your return rocket needs steady electrical cooling power!
choiceA.imageCaption: This illustration shows a concept of how the NASA Mars Ascent Vehicle, carrying tubes containing rock and soil samples, could be launched from the surface of Mars in one step of the Mars sample return mission.

choiceB.description: Tap battery reserves to run oxygen generators at high output so cabin air feels crisp and energizing.
choiceB.outcomeText: Fresh oxygen hisses through every vent and perks up the crew, while your Sol 1 battery surplus drops sharply.
choiceB.nasaRealDecision: Aboard NASA's Perseverance rover, the toaster-sized MOXIE experiment proved humans can extract pure breathable O2 straight from Mars's 95% CO2 atmosphere—though running its high-temperature solid oxide cells demands heavy electricity.
choiceB.nasaFactEmphasis: On Mars, the air is 95% carbon dioxide. MOXIE heats and splits CO2 molecules into pure oxygen gas and carbon monoxide.
choiceB.imageCaption: MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) was launched aboard NASA's Perseverance rover to test a technology for extracting oxygen from the Red Planet's carbon dioxide-rich atmosphere.

choiceC.description: Power up the high-gain dish for storm tracking while sealing astronauts inside the cozy central dome.
choiceC.outcomeText: Crisp orbital radar helps the crew plan safely indoors, though running the big dish heater dips your battery meter.
choiceC.nasaComparisonTitle: Orbital Weather & Deep Space Relay
choiceC.nasaRealDecision: During June 2018, NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the storm growing from local to planet-wide, giving scientists early warning while serving as the primary radio relay between surface rovers and Earth's Deep Space Network.
choiceC.nasaFactEmphasis: Mars orbiters track dust opacity (tau) and beam surface telemetry to Earth's 70-meter Deep Space Network antennas across a 22-minute light-time gap.
choiceC.imageCaption: Workers at NASA Deep Space Network Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex prepare a support leg that would help raise a portion of the giant Mars antenna.

realLifeComparison.title: Compare Your Future 2038 Mission to Real 2018 NASA Science

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: In June 2018, NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover lost 97% of its sunlight, couldn't recharge, and froze in the dark after 14 years on Mars. Across the planet, Curiosity kept working right through the storm because it carried a small nuclear battery (an MMRTG).
cards.howItConnectsToGame: NASA's future Mars bases plan to pair solar arrays with compact nuclear fission reactors—just like your 2038 base needed both to survive 10 Sols!

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: NASA's weather instruments on Curiosity proved a surprising twist: while 2018 dust storms made Mars days cooler by blocking sunlight, they made Mars nights WARMER because dust trapped heat near the ground.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Midway through the storm, dialing down heaters worked because suspended red dust acted like a giant blanket over Mars.

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: Because Mars is millions of miles away, radio messages in 2018 took 6 to 22 minutes each way—up to 44 minutes just to ask a question and hear an answer.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Every compromise you made had ripple effects days later—just like real astronauts must survive on their own choices before Earth even knows!
